Twenty Sixth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2008
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 24, pp 159-180
Project Report on Vicarious Calibration of AWiFS
Sensor of Resourcesat-1 with Antarctica as a
Natural Test-Site
S. S. Manjul
SSD/EOSG, Space Applications Centre (ISRO), Ahmedabad 380 015, India
ABSTRACT
This report describes the project activities performed under the 26 th Indian
Scientific Expedition to Antarctica. Under the project, four different types of
Ground Truth Radiometers were designed and developed indigenously. These
instruments consist in all 32 spectral bands covering the spectral range from 400
to 2500-nm. Among the 32 bands, four spectral bands are identical to that of
AWiFS sensor. These instruments were successfully operated under harsh and
hostile environment of Antarctica and they were used for collecting voluminous
ground truth data during the period from December 2006 to March 2007. The
data was collected concurrently/non-concurrently with Resources at-1 passes.
The data was collected at ground level with the height ranging from 1 to 2 meter
and also at helicopter level with the altitude ranging from 200 to 3000-m. The
measured data consists of spectral reflectance/reflected spectral radiance of
various terrain surfaces covering snow/ice, water bodies, rocks and soil. It also
consists of measurement of direct and direct-plus-diffused components of
incoming solar spectral irradiance. Images of AWiFS were acquired over the test
site nearer to Sankalp area. The calibration methodology has been successfully
established. The methodology essentially consists of estimation of spectral
radiance at the entrance port of the AWiFS sensor by using the measured values
of reflected spectral radiance from the ice surface and water bodies at ground
as well as the altitude of 3000 m and the estimation of the values of path
radiance above 3000 m by modeling the atmosphere over the test site. Test
results show that in December, Antarctica provides constant illumination-
geometry conditions where the spectral irradiance remains constant within ± 3 %
for the duration of 3 hours at the time of polar satellite passes. This time period
is adequate to perform ground truth data collection experiments concurrent with
the satellite passes. It was observed that during December - February more cloud
free days are available. It was also observed that the optical depths of the
atmosphere are stable, predictable and accountable. AWiFS imagery shows the
spatial non-uniformity of about 3% within the surface area of about 5 x 5-km
2.
160
Finally, it has been demonstrated that Antarctica has very stable Land-Atmosphere
system and is a unique natural test-site to perform validation and vicarious
radiometric calibration of a space borne optical sensors.
Keywords: Vicarious calibration, Post-flight radiometric calibration, Resourcesat-
1, Radiometry, Ground Truth Radiometer, Spectral Signature Studies, Remote
Sensing, Radiometry, Optical sensors, Snow, Ice, Polar Remote Sensing,
Antarctica.
INTRODUCTION
Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) has launched a series
of remote sensing satellites that incorporate state-of-art technology. They
are being extensively used for monitoring and managing the earth’s
natural resources. Among these satellites, Resourcesat-1 has produced
voluminous and useful data for various types of remote sensing
applications.
Radiometric calibration of satellite sensors is a key to providing
long-term continuous, reliable and consistent data sets for various remote
sensing applications. Pre-flight calibration is carried out in the controlled
environment of the laboratory against standard calibrated sources which
are traceable to international standards. In general, in-flight calibration
of a sensor is performed with several mechanisms. Most of the modern
sensors have built-in calibration mechanism consisting of the sources
such as light emitting diodes, black bodies, tungsten-halogen lamps etc.
(Lyu et al., 2000; Hugh et al., 2005). The implementation of built-in
calibration mechanisms may be prone to its own degradation and involves
extra cost and complexity. The in-flight calibration is done by means of
independent check, by using natural sources such as sun or moon (Hugh
et al., 2005). However, it demands pointing capability of sensors towards
the natural sources during calibration process. The techniques to perform
the in-flight calibration, known as vicarious calibration, involve estimation
of calibration coefficient ([mw/cm
2-sr-ì]/[mv]) with a different
methodology than that is used for pre-flight calibration. Normally, the
methodology involves the use of either natural or artificial terrain
surfaces. The artificial surface could be fabricated, characterized, and
used by illuminating with solar radiations. However, the feasible and
cost effective solution for undertaking vicarious radiometric calibration
is to use a natural test site such as water bodies, sand dunes etc.
